body.heading: The switching tax
paragraphs: Every time you jump between homework, messages and a video, your brain pays a small switching cost to reload what it was doing. Researchers who study attention describe this leftover pull as attention residue — part of your mind stays stuck on the previous thing.
You can feel it yourself: after checking a message mid-task, the next sentence or sum takes longer to come back. Nothing is wrong with you. That is simply how attention works.

body.heading: Try single-tasking in small doses
paragraphs: Pick one task and give it a short, protected window — fifteen or twenty minutes. Close the other tabs, or at least mute them. When an unrelated thought pops up, jot it on paper instead of acting on it, then return.
Single-tasking is a skill, not a personality trait. Short, regular practice windows build it far better than one heroic afternoon of forced concentration.

takeaway: One thing, briefly and fully, beats five things at once.
